item.title: Global ice-cliff survey tests disputed theory behind projections of accelerated sea level rise
item.description: A new study led by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) provides the most comprehensive observational analysis yet of the towering ice cliffs that fringe Earth's ice sheets, giving scientists new evidence to evaluate a long-debated process that could influence future sea level rise. Improving these projections is increasingly important as rising seas threaten coastal communities and infrastructure worldwide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: I discovered a Roman fort in Wales—it may hold the key to the ancient Welsh legend of Macsen Wledig
item.description: My recent discovery of a Roman fort and its extraordinary connection with medieval folklore was the fruition of many hours of painstaking research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild birds rewrite rules of flight efficiency: Study reveals power of 'free fuel' from the sky
item.description: An international study has overturned a longstanding textbook view of how much energy animals use to travel, revealing that flying can sometimes be cheaper than swimming. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Americans who go to church and trust science are also more likely to believe in ghosts and curses, research shows
item.description: Americans who trust science and reason more than their churches' teachings, but still believe in God or attend services, are also more likely to believe in magic than those who prioritize religious teachings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply
item.description: From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy. Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration. Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Penelope Lauren Garcia-Galan

item.title: India's cobras share genetic ties across the mainland, while Sri Lankan cobras form a distinct genetic lineage
item.description: The spectacled cobra (Naja naja) is one of India's "big four" snakes responsible for most serious snakebite cases. It is currently considered one species, which lives across much of South Asia, with regional differences in color, hood markings and venom. However, it's still unclear which regional cobra populations represent separate evolutionary groups. A new study published in Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution has helped parse out which groups have different lineages, and when and where they may have diverged from their ancestors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Young voters fear mass shootings but are divided on gun control
item.description: Nearly 50 million Americans ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and about 60% say they plan to. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live
item.description: Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: "Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?" Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
item.description: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket Lab announces another delay for its medium-lift Neutron rocket
item.description: Rocket Lab announced the Neutron rocket in 2021, aiming for a first flight in 2024. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
item.description: A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Transit, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations. Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gianine Figliozzi

item.title: Palm-leaf manuscripts reveal traces of their preparation through X-rays and machine learning
item.description: For centuries, people across South and Southeast Asia recorded religious teachings, literary works, legal regulations and scientific knowledge on palm leaves. Before they could be inscribed or written on, the leaves had to undergo extensive preparation, with processing techniques varying across regions and potentially leaving distinct material signatures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: WHO urges action on lead poisoning dangers
item.description: The World Health Organization on Thursday told countries to do more to prevent lead exposure, with hundreds of millions of children affected worldwide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What’s your favorite mnemonic for remembering the order of the planets?
item.description: What’s your favorite mnemonic for remembering the order of the planets? My Very Educated Mother Just Showed Us Nine Planets... back when Pluto was considered a planet Ver más comentarios Sylvia Ramos Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: How did early Māori society develop? New research reveals a clearer timeline
item.description: When the first Polynesian settlers arrived in Aotearoa New Zealand some 750 years ago, they found an environment very different from the lands they left behind. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chandra breaks down 'Treble Clef's' galaxy cluster collision
item.description: Astronomers have used NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the "Treble Clef" because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Welcomes All Ages, Experience Levels for Space Apps Challenge
item.description: Registration is open for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, a two-day global event on Saturday, Nov. 14 and Sunday, Nov. 15, where teams work to create solutions inspired by NASA’s most ambitious exploration goals and making use of the agency’s free and open data. The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: AI helps detect media bias, informing voters and news consumers
item.description: In 2024, a collaborative Penn venture introduced a more objective way for people to examine how different outlets cover the same events and ultimately decide how they perceive and use information shared in the media. The Media Bias Detector, conceived in Penn's Computational Social Science (CSS) Lab, a joint venture of Penn Engineering, the Annenberg School for Communication and the Wharton School, uses artificial intelligence to analyze news articles for characteristics including topic, tone, political lean, and the facts and people included in coverage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mass shooting survivors' memories are full of sensory detail, both positive and negative
item.description: It was perhaps fitting, in a twisted, only-in-America way. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Awards Enable Research, Technology to Build Future Workforce
item.description: NASA has selected 12 U.S. institutions to receive $12 million to accelerate academic research and technology development in support of the agency’s priorities for exploring the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Through NASA’s Minority University Research and Education Project (MUREP) Space Technology Artemis Research (M‑STAR) initiative, selected institutions will each receive up to $1 million […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sandra May

item.title: Why are pets scared of fireworks?
item.description: Fireworks are an integral part of many celebrations and cultural events. With their pretty colors, spectacular sights and big bangs, fireworks are a popular attraction for many people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
item.description: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Los expertos lo tienen claro: "Los que beben café tienen un microbioma intestinal más diverso que los que no beben café"
item.description: Durante años, la ciencia ha intentado desentrañar los secretos del café, buscando justificar nuestro 'amor' por tomar a diario esta bebida que a veces ha sido demonizada. Y es que, entre los muchos beneficios que tiene, destaca uno que se está investigando ahora mucho mejor, y hablamos justamente de la alteración que hace sobre nuestra microbiota. Pero casi siempre para nuestro bien. Unas bacterias. El gran protagonista de esta historia es un estudio publicado en el año 2024 en el que participó el conocido epidemiólogo genético Tim Spector. En este se analizaron datos de más de 22.000… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Solving the mystery behind a flightless beetle's transatlantic journey
item.description: They can't fly or swim, so why do their closest relatives appear on different continents? Grey Gustafson, an associate professor in the Department of Biological Sciences, discovered through DNA sequencing that the ancestors of some of today's tiger beetles existed in South America and Africa before the two continents separated. What's more, North America's largest tiger beetles are related to these ancestral South American giant tiger beetles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two decades of publications reveal research institutions becoming more alike worldwide
item.description: Where researchers go, their knowledge goes. And that shapes where innovation happens. "Recruiting researchers is one way institutions gain new knowledge and steer their research in particular directions," explains Vito D. P. Servedio, senior scientist at CSH. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fatal Neanderthal wound may be earliest evidence of a wooden spear attack on a human ancestor
item.description: A round hole in the shoulder blade (scapula) of a Neanderthal whose partial remains were unearthed in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan may be the earliest known example of lethal interpersonal violence with a wooden spear in the hominin fossil record. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Remains may be earliest evidence of ancient human speared to death
item.description: A round hole in the shoulder blade of a Neanderthal fossil could be the earliest known evidence of ancient humans attacking one another with wooden spears, researchers say. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Jacinta Bowler

item.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance
item.description: NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the Moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the Moon’s surface. Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected. In particular, NASA measured whether the thermal protection […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Elyna Niles-Carnes

item.title: Scientific expertise does not guarantee greater credibility in public debates, survey suggests
item.description: A study of more than 6,000 people in the U.K. and Sweden suggests that although scientists are generally regarded as credible, their status as experts is more contested when they discuss issues such as health, education and employment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: America’s love of sports betting is linked to a spike in antidepressant use, study finds
item.description: Legalizing sports betting has been tied to a 60 percent increase in gambling disorder cases Fuente: The Independent - World.
item.dc:creator: Julia Musto

item.title: New smart patch could help detect and treat blood clots after spinal surgery
item.description: Blood clots that develop after spinal surgery can lead to serious complications. When blood accumulates around the spinal cord, it may increase pressure on surrounding nerves, potentially causing severe pain, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Early detection and timely treatment are therefore essential. However, continuously monitoring these complications remains challenging, and conventional treatments may require additional surgery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil footprints reveal how dinosaur ancestors gradually shifted from sprawling to upright walking
item.description: A research team led by Dr. Lorenzo Marchetti of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin described the earliest archosauriform footprints (Pachychirotherium gardenaensis) from the GEOPARC Bletterbach—UNESCO World Heritage Dolomites, Italy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chandra Finds Possible Origin of ‘Treble Clef’ Waves
item.description: A formation of radio waves looks remarkably like a treble clef in this Oct. 14, 2026, image from NASA’s Chandra X-Ray Observatory. Researchers used Chandra to find that the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters. Read more about this discovery. […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Drowned 5,000-year-old forests reborn as thriving peat reefs and biodiversity hotspots off Mozambique
item.description: Researchers from the Bazaruto Center for Scientific Studies (BCSS) Ocean Observatory have documented ancient forests that grew on the Mozambican coast thousands of years ago and have been found beneath the sea, where they now serve as hotspots teeming with marine life similar in biodiversity to coral reefs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China is a beacon of global embryo research, says scientist on return from US to lead lab
item.description: Leading life scientist Wu Jun, who recently left the United States to return to his homeland, believes many of the world’s top embryo researchers are now working in China. Wu, well known for his stem cell research, particularly related to the stem cell-derived embryo model, is speaking in an office at Westlake University, in Hangzhou in the eastern province of Zhejiang. Some of his belongings remain in bags placed haphazardly on a nearby cabinet, waiting to be unpacked. “This is just a temporary... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Dannie Peng

item.title: Pupil size reveals differences between speaking aloud and inner speech
item.description: Even when we are silent, we often talk to ourselves in our heads, using words to guide our thoughts and actions. This "inner speech" is thought to be involved in thinking and self-control. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Research finds vegan honey could be made with similar antimicrobial properties to mānuka honey
item.description: Vegan honey alternatives could be engineered to have antimicrobial properties similar to those of prized mānuka honey from New Zealand, according to research at Aston University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fun fact: DART didn't just hit Dimorphos, it shortened its orbit by about 32 minutes. Humanity's first successful asteroid nudge, and it was a very polite shove. Can't wait to…
item.description: Fun fact: DART didn't just hit Dimorphos, it shortened its orbit by about 32 minutes. Humanity's first successful asteroid nudge, and it was a very polite shove. Can't wait to watch this one! Funny time Fuente: NASA.

item.description: Have you heard about #HauntedAppalachia? Legend has it the forest is full of cryptids and the paranormal—eerie stories set in the Appalachian Mountains... Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Cortisol is a reproduction friend, not enemy
item.description: A major international study of the role cortisol plays in reproduction has found it may not be the villain it has been depicted as, and it may actually promote healthy reproduction. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Finding new ways to catch a thief—via intruders' airborne eDNA
item.description: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is increasingly being investigated by forensic scientists as a tool to help solve criminal cases that lack biological traces—and attention is also turning to collecting trace airborne eDNA left behind by intruders in residential burglaries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Time to redefine concept of health: Indigenous views of health reveal gaps in Western health frameworks
item.description: How health is defined, measured and addressed by Indigenous communities doesn't match Western frameworks, leading health systems to fall short in caring for vulnerable communities, a University of Otago—Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka–led study has found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
item.description: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Arctic sea ice hits another troubling low in 2026
item.description: Arctic sea ice is shrinking in both winter and summer, with satellite records revealing that the region's remaining ice is becoming thinner, younger, and more vulnerable to melting. Despite a recent slowdown in summer losses, scientists warn that the Arctic could experience a nearly ice-free summer before 2050. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why tightly confined water's response to electric fields depends on direction
item.description: Using an advanced new mathematical model, a pair of physicists in Belgium has revealed the origins of an unusual, direction-dependent effect found in water confined to a narrow gap between two plates. Through research published in Physical Review Letters, Mehdi Neek-Amal and Francois Peeters at the University of Antwerp showed how two drastically different dielectric responses in this water emerge from the natural bonding behavior of its molecules. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Expanding climate models to better capture the complexities of public health
item.description: About a decade ago, a group of climate scientists described five scenarios for the future. Called the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), these scenarios suggest how socioeconomic development could evolve in worlds with differing challenges to climate adaptation and mitigation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eating late at night linked to up to 30% higher risk of liver disease
item.description: Eating late at night could be putting your liver at risk, according to a large study led by Oregon Health & Science University. Researchers analyzed data from nearly 200,000 people and found that those who regularly ate after dinner or around bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, including fatty liver disease and cirrhosis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New research challenges the idea that GST always hits lower-income households hardest
item.description: Goods and services tax (GST) is priced into many everyday purchases, from groceries and clothing to restaurant meals and household bills. That means any change to the tax can affect how much households have left to spend. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI
item.description: Huang told CNBC he has ongoing "dialogs" with researchers in China. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Turning up the heat on chickpea yield
item.description: A University of Queensland study has outlined a practical pathway for accelerating the development of heat-adapted chickpeas using data from new 'omic' technologies. Ph.D. candidate Callum Jamie said the suite of technologies offered tremendous opportunities to understand how a complex trait like heat tolerance works. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
item.description: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Looking for relief from dating app anxiety? Try a variety of platforms
item.description: Using more than one type of app, including both mainstream apps such as Tinder or Hinge and gay apps like Grindr, could lead to lower levels of anxiety among gay men who use mobile dating platforms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Early growth differences help explain which beech trees survive forest competition
item.description: The fight for survival in the forest is fierce: light, water and nutrients are all limited. This is particularly true in "mast years"—times when trees and shrubs produce an unusually large crop of fruits, nuts or seeds. Then the race for growth is on. But can differences in height between trees in their first year of life make a difference to their future, even if these differences are just one or two centimeters (0.4 or 0.8 inches)? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Green space is linked with fewer gun-related homicides—but not everywhere
item.description: Physical surroundings affect everything from personal well-being to a neighborhood's safety. A new study from The Ohio State University finds that when it comes to preventing gun violence in a community, green space can help, but its location makes a big difference. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum sensor could measure how Earth drags spacetime
item.description: Einstein's theory of general relativity describes gravity as the bending of spacetime, a mathematical model that combines three-dimensional space and time into a single, four-dimensional continuum. The theory also predicts that a rotating object, such as Earth, slightly drags the surrounding spacetime as it rotates, a phenomenon known as frame-dragging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
item.description: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Hong Kong ranks third globally as philanthropy hub, behind New York and Seoul, study finds
item.description: Hong Kong has emerged as the third best city in the world for wealthy individuals seeking to make philanthropic contributions over the medium term, trailing New York and Seoul, according to a study by Altrata. The inaugural Giving Opportunity Index by the US-based group that tracks the world’s affluent population ranked 100 cities based on three criteria: wealth, donor affinity and philanthropic infrastructure. The study defined the “global wealthy” as individuals with a net worth of more than... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Cheryl Arcibal

item.title: Countries most vulnerable to fossil fuel phaseout generate just 6% of global output, climate analysis finds
item.description: Countries highly vulnerable to the phase-out of oil, gas and coal account for just 6% of global economic output, countries in Africa stand to benefit from their vast solar energy potential, and the economic interests of the U.S., Europe and China are affected by climate policy in surprisingly similar ways. A study by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) published in Nature Sustainability now shows, for 169 countries around the world, how the fight against global heating affects national assets—and what geopolitical challenges and opportunities arise as a result. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ascension Island: How a planting project created a lush cloud forest
item.description: In the middle of nowhere, a small island emerges in the Atlantic Ocean. This unique territory completely changed in the 19th century thanks to the efforts of two British scientists: Charles Darwin and Joseph Dalton Hooker, researchers who stopped at the British naval base and documented the island during their expeditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could the dodo return? US firm maps 95% of its genome and identifies gene-editing targets
item.description: Colossal Biosciences aims to resurrect the extinct dodo bird using cutting-edge gene-editing technologies. By leveraging their sophisticated AI platform, GenoMorph, the company has pinpointed essential genetic traits. With 95% of the dodo genome analysis complete, their ambitious project is on track, though a specific timeline for the living dodo remains undisclosed. This groundbreaking venture is part of a larger initiative to counteract the effects of human-induced species extinction. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Archaeologists find 19 injuries in 12 people buried in Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia
item.description: Archaeologists found evidence of traumatic injuries in 12 individuals from Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia. These injuries were discovered in domestic spaces like houses, pits, and wells across various sites. Examination of the remains revealed sharp-force and blunt-force injuries indicating potential violence in their lives. Researchers proposed that social conditions may have contributed to the unusual burial practices observed. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Montana rancher’s rare Nanotyrannus fossil goes on display ahead of $9M auction
item.description: A rare find in the form of a nearly 70 percent complete Nanotyrannus skeleton, affectionately named Jodi, has been unearthed by rancher Jodi Pierson in Montana and is set to go under the hammer at Sotheby’s in New York on October 27. This well-preserved specimen is anticipated to garner between $6 million and $9 million, creating a buzz among paleontologists and collectors alike due to its invaluable significance. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Strokes have nearly doubled among younger adults, and scientists aren't sure why
item.description: Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades. Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Tech Aids Lost Birdsong Recovery: Synthetic calls help sparrows relearn old songs; scientists weigh AI’s role
item.description: A groundbreaking approach has emerged, leveraging computer-generated recordings to rejuvenate the bird songs that nature has lost. Researchers successfully reintroduced the unique call of the rufous-collared sparrow back into its habitat in Argentina. This innovative conservation strategy seeks to bolster endangered species by preserving their vocal heritage and fostering communication skills, as demonstrated by positive outcomes in captive breeding for species such as the regent honeyeater. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to rare risk of sudden vision loss
item.description: Popular diabetes and weight loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy have been linked to a slightly increased risk of a rare condition that can cause sudden, potentially permanent vision loss. Although the risk remains very low, Rutgers researchers say the findings warrant attention as millions of people turn to GLP-1 medications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. The Milky […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Fires Arrive in the Amazon Rainforest
item.description: During El Niño, a cascade of fires across the tropics begins in equatorial Asia and continues in the central and eastern Amazon. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Consumers need clearer answers before they can trust precision fermentation, new report finds
item.description: Consumers may not fully understand precision fermentation yet, but many are curious enough to taste the results. New qualitative research from the EIT Food Consumer Observatory, published ahead of World Food Day on Oct. 16, suggests that this curiosity creates an important opportunity for food innovation, provided companies can answer consumers' questions clearly and deliver on the first bite. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Now you see them: Researchers uncover patterns in vessels that vanish at sea
item.description: Across the waters of West Africa, commercial fishing vessels vanish along international boundary lines. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists alarmed as super El Niño collides with 'strange uptick' in Galapagos iguana trafficking
item.description: The only lizard in the world that can live and forage at sea may now be in a fight for survival. International scientists warn black-market trafficking of Galapagos marine iguanas is peaking just as the super El Niño decimates their natural food source. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate adaptation's delivery gap: Turning national plans into action
item.description: By 2025, 143 of 154 developing countries had a National Adaptation Plan process in place, yet implementation has not kept pace. Many countries still lack the institutional capacity, project preparation and finance needed to turn their priorities into strategies, bankable projects and results on the ground. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Social service agencies need safeguards when using AI
item.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used by social service agencies to handle cases involving child abuse, intimate partner violence and elder abuse. But a University of Iowa researcher and former social worker says the agencies need to establish safeguards to ensure that AI technology does not lead to bias against vulnerable or disadvantaged populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can AI feel safer than human advice for consumers who face discrimination?
item.description: What should you cook for dinner on a budget of 20 euros when you have a guest with a gluten intolerance? A shopper might ask a shop assistant for advice or consult, for example, Hopla, the AI-powered shopping assistant launched by French supermarket chain Carrefour. Behind this everyday choice lies a broader question: when faced with a recommendation, who do we trust more? A human being or an AI? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
item.description: A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Fair climate transitions need more than financial support, evidence review suggests
item.description: The transition to a low-carbon economy will not affect all people and places equally. Although its overall benefits may outweigh its costs, workers may lose jobs, households may face higher prices and communities dependent on carbon-intensive industries may experience lasting economic and social disruption. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Green, pink and purple: Astronomers reveal the surprising true colors of white dwarf stars
item.description: University of Warwick astronomers have shown that white dwarf stars can glow in a range of colors, including the first star ever found that would appear green to the human eye. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers in exile thrive in new academic settings when they contribute knowledge, not just receive aid
item.description: Publishing scientific articles requires more than knowledge of academic writing conventions; it also depends on access to networks that support the research and publication process. Academic networks provide opportunities to exchange knowledge, receive feedback and develop collaborations that can strengthen both research and careers. For researchers in vulnerable situations, such connections can be crucial. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA develops batteries to power humanity's return to moon
item.description: If you've ever had your car start sluggishly, or not at all, on a particularly frigid winter morning, you know standard batteries do not like extreme cold. That's why NASA researchers are working to develop a battery that could function in the brutal cold of the moon's south pole, where nighttime temperatures plunge to minus 328 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 200 degrees Celsius). Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
item.description: A groundbreaking study suggests that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization, far more than previously believed. Researchers estimate that 93% of this population was lost within 73 years, revealing a demographic catastrophe on a scale that dramatically changes our understanding of Australian history. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

Which makes sense because the spacecraft launched is headed for the ISS and the timing of the launch must be such that it matches the ISS orbital plane alignment.

item.title: Uganda's sugarcane boom leaves families hungry: What needs to change
item.description: Busoga, in eastern Uganda, is a low, fertile plateau surrounded on three sides by Lake Victoria, the Nile River and Lake Kyoga. Most of its 4.3 million people farm small, rain-fed plots. Yet hunger is common: in the 2024 census, about a third of Busoga households reported going whole days without food. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fine particles from aircraft exhaust become more harmful over time, lab tests suggest
item.description: Fine particulate matter consists of tiny particles with diameters in the nanometer range. They are produced, for example, by fuel combustion, remain suspended in the air and can penetrate deep into the respiratory tract. There, they can trigger oxidative stress, a process that promotes inflammation and, over the long term, can lead to serious health problems such as respiratory or cardiovascular diseases. Scientists call this harmful property the particles' oxidative potential. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New chip-scale gyroscope measures rotation with unprecedented sensitivity
item.description: Researchers have developed a chip-scale optical ring-laser gyroscope that can measure rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour. This record sensitivity, approaching Earth's rotation rate of 15 degrees per hour, could eventually be useful for precision navigation and orientation systems, particularly where GPS is unavailable. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A trip to Mars could come at a heartbreaking cost
item.description: When astronauts first travel to Mars or anywhere else in deep space, they will have to contend with two problems that our planet protects us from on its surface—radiation and weightlessness. Scientists already know both can have a profound impact on the human body, but the extent of that impact and how long it can last remain a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
item.description: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Urbanization takes a bigger toll on bird diversity in the tropics than it does at other latitudes, study finds
item.description: Researchers at McGill University have found that urbanization is weakening one of Earth's most enduring ecological patterns: the tendency for biodiversity to increase toward the tropics, a pattern known as the latitudinal diversity gradient. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When parents don't see eye to eye: Are differences in parenting styles a bad thing?
item.description: Sometimes it can be hard for parents to agree on how to raise children. One parent might insist their child's homework has to be finished before they're allowed to use devices. The other may think a bit of screen time before studying is perfectly reasonable. Rules and consequences might be the preferred strategy of one parent, while the other favors a more flexible approach. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket Lab’s stock slides as the company pushes back Neutron’s first launch
item.description: Neutron, a medium-lift rocket meant to rival SpaceX’s Falcon 9, will no longer launch this year. Fuente: MarketWatch.
item.dc:creator: William Gavin

item.title: Waste plastics become molecular sponges that capture water from air
item.description: Discarded plastic packaging materials, old CDs and even LEGO bricks can be transformed into materials that capture significant amounts of moisture from the air. Materials chemists Anastasiia Naryshkina, Paul Schweng and Robert Woodward at the University of Vienna have converted several types of plastic waste into water-attracting polymer networks that take up water even in dry climates and release it again under moderate heating, for example, using sunlight. The study, published in Chem Circularity, offers a route to give plastic waste a second life as an adsorbent for atmospheric water… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Spawning coral release quintillions of eggs each year, new calculations suggest
item.description: Most kinds of coral spawn once a year. In an enormous multiday event synchronized to specific phases of the moon, they release vast slicks of eggs and sperm into the ocean to be mixed together by the drifting currents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
item.description: A major study found that several cancers are rising faster among younger adults in England, even as smoking, diet, and other established risk factors have generally improved. Excess weight explains only part of the increase, leaving scientists searching for other possible causes, including changes in the gut microbiome and early-life exposures. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Genome publishing overhaul targets 200 reports per month, up from 30
item.description: The Wellcome Sanger Institute's Tree of Life program plans to accelerate publication of genome notes from approximately 30 per month to 200, expanding access to research that is supporting advances in agriculture, conservation and medicine. This increase will be facilitated by a new specialized workflow developed by F1000 and the Wellcome Sanger Institute for Wellcome Open Research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A single carbon atom stitches flat molecules into 3D structures
item.description: Flat is fine for a sheet of paper, but many of the most useful molecules need depth. Now, researchers from Japan have found a way to give them that depth using nothing more than a single carbon atom. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How E. coli eavesdrops on the metabolic activity of other gut bacteria
item.description: The gut microbiome is teeming with hundreds of bacterial species and trillions of bacteria. These microorganisms influence many aspects of health, including digestion, and assist with numerous functions in the body. Gut bacteria compete for the limited nutrients available in their environment, while also interacting with each other in ways that can influence the stability of the microbial community. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From 'A Little Princess' to 'Black Panther,' how Hollywood films have reimagined the South Asian epic 'Ramayana'
item.description: American audiences will be able to watch an English-dubbed version of "Ramayana," a Hindi film based on a South Asian epic tradition, in theaters in November 2026. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How detection dogs are helping protect one of Australia's most imperiled lizards
item.description: Many of the Australian animals most at risk of extinction are extremely tough to track down. That's because they live in small pockets of disappearing nature, such as rare grasslands or ancient forests, in worryingly low numbers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists identify avian cholera as major cause of penguin deaths in Antarctica
item.description: Thousands of Adélie penguins found dead in Antarctica in 2024 were primarily victims of avian cholera, not high pathogenicity avian influenza (H5N1) as researchers initially suspected, according to a study published today in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. The findings highlight an underrecognized threat to Antarctic wildlife and the importance of comprehensive disease investigations, particularly as H5N1 continues to raise concerns for seabird and marine mammal populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Engineered enzyme could improve detection of HIV and other viruses
item.description: Scientists have long used a powerful gene-editing tool called CRISPR to make precise changes to DNA. But a different version of the technology, known as Cas13a, targets RNA, the genetic material found in viruses such as HIV. Now, researchers at Rice University have developed an improved version of Cas13a that could make it easier to detect HIV and other RNA viruses in blood and environmental samples. The study was published in Cell Chemical Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Firms facing tariff shocks choose collaboration over conquest
item.description: New research has charted the way U.S. businesses adapted to market shocks caused by reductions in import tariffs and increased foreign competition, with greater innovation emerging as a longer-term benefit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI-assisted math advance highlights gap between finding answers and judging their significance
item.description: AI models are good at finding answers to mathematical puzzles but are not as good at research judgment, according to theoretical computer scientists. Fuente: Phys.org.
